summary.text: Salinity is the amount of salt dissolved in water, usually measured in grams of salt per litre or per kilogram of water.
Along with temperature and pressure, it governs the water's density and heat capacity, which matter for ocean currents and heat exchange with the atmosphere.
Seawater typically holds about 35 g/kg, rivers and lakes range from under 0.01 g/kg to a few g/kg, and the Dead Sea tops 200 g/kg.

Carbon dioxide

items.explain: Dissolved oxygen and nitrogen are not usually included, but carbon dioxide is often counted because it partly turns into carbonates and bicarbonates.

items.explain: Natural waters contain a complex mixture of many elements from different sources in different molecular forms, which makes exact measurement difficult.

beats.title: How Salty Is Salty?
beats.hook: Rain, rivers, the open sea and the Dead Sea all carry salt, but in wildly different amounts that help steer the oceans.

beats.prompt: Match each water to its typical salt content
beats.explain: Seawater sits near 35 g/kg, fresh waters hold far less, rain and snow carry very little, and the Dead Sea holds several times more than the ocean.

beats.prompt: Two labs measure salinity in the same sample of water, one filtering it at 0.45 μm and the other at 0.2 μm. How far apart are their results?
beats.explain: Dissolved matter is defined as what passes a very fine filter, and whichever pore size is used, the salinity value varies by no more than a few percent.

choices.label: The coarser filter finds no salt
choices.feedback: Dissolved salt passes through both filters, so both still measure it.

choices.label: Within a few percent of each other
One reads about double the other
choices.feedback: Filter size changes what counts as dissolved only slightly, not by a factor of two.

choices.label: Only the finer filter finds salt
choices.feedback: Both pore sizes let dissolved matter through, so both detect salt.

beats.prompt: Sort each dissolved substance by whether salinity usually counts it
beats.explain: Salinity is the dissolved salt content, such as sodium chloride and magnesium sulfate; carbon dioxide is often included because it partly becomes carbonates, while oxygen and nitrogen gases usually are not.

paragraphs.heading: What salinity measures
paragraphs.text: Salinity is how much salt is dissolved in water. Salts are compounds such as sodium chloride and magnesium sulfate that split into ions when they dissolve. Salinity is usually given in grams of salt per litre or per kilogram of water. A contour line linking points of equal salinity is called an isohaline.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Salinity shapes much of the chemistry of natural waters and the living processes in them. Together with temperature and pressure, it sets physical traits of water such as its density and heat capacity. Those traits in turn help explain ocean currents and how the sea trades heat with the air.

paragraphs.heading: Salty, fresh and in between
paragraphs.text: Seawater usually holds about 35 g/kg of salt, with lower values near coasts where rivers flow in. Rivers and lakes vary widely, from under 0.01 g/kg to a few g/kg, and some places are saltier still. The Dead Sea has more than 200 g/kg. Rain and other precipitation usually carry 20 mg/kg or less of dissolved material.

paragraphs.heading: Simple idea, hard to measure
paragraphs.text: The idea of salinity is simple, but defining and measuring it precisely is hard. Natural waters hold a complex mix of many elements in different forms, and not all of them come from dissolved salts. Many are difficult to measure accurately, and a full chemical analysis is impractical when there are many samples. So in practice, salinity is tied to the total of a set of dissolved ingredients, often eight major ions, with seven minor ones added for seawater at the highest precision. Scientists studying the deep ocean compare results to almost five significant digits, using a bottled product called IAPSO Standard Seawater to keep their measurements consistent.

paragraphs.heading: Changing ways to measure
paragraphs.text: Before the 1980s, salinity was mostly measured by titration. Adding silver nitrate revealed the amount of halide ions, mainly chlorine and bromine, giving a value called chlorinity, which was then multiplied by a factor to cover everything else. The results, called Knudsen salinities, were written in parts per thousand (ppt or ‰). Later, measuring how well seawater conducts electricity led to the practical salinity scale 1978, or PSS-78, whose values have no units. People sometimes write PSU after the number, but this is formally incorrect and strongly discouraged.

paragraphs.heading: One sample, three numbers
paragraphs.text: In 2010, a new seawater standard called TEOS-10 proposed absolute salinity as a replacement for practical salinity. Absolute salinity is a mass fraction, in grams per kilogram of solution. It is found by combining conductivity readings with information about regional differences in seawater makeup, or by measuring density directly. The scales line up closely: a typical seawater sample with a chlorinity of 19.37 ppt has a Knudsen salinity of 35.00 ppt, a practical salinity of about 35.0, and an absolute salinity of about 35.2 g/kg.
